In [[geometry]] of 4 dimensions, a '''3-4 duoprism''', the second smallest p-q [[duoprism]], is a [[4-polytope]] resulting from the [[Cartesian product]] of a [[triangle]] and a [[square]].

The ''3-4 duoprism'' exists in some of the [[Uniform 5-polytope#The B5 family|uniform 5-polytopes in the B5 family]].

== Related complex polygons==
[[File:Complex_polygon_3x4_stereographic3.svg|160px|thumb|Stereographic projection of complex polygon, <sub>3</sub>{}×<sub>4</sub>{} has 12 vertices and 7 3-edges, shown here with 4 red triangular 3-edges and 3 blue square 4-edges.]]
The quasiregular [[complex polytope]] <sub>3</sub>{}×<sub>4</sub>{}, {{CDD|3node_1|2|4node_1}}, in <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> has a real representation as a 3-4 [[duoprism]] in 4-dimensional space. It has 12 vertices, and 4 3-edges and 3 4-edges. Its symmetry is <sub>3</sub>[2]<sub>4</sub>, order 12.<ref>[[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|Coxeter, H. S. M.]]; ''Regular Complex Polytopes'', Cambridge University Press, (1974).</ref>

=== 3-4 duopyramid ===
{| class="wikitable" align="right" width=300
!bgcolor=#e7dcc3 colspan=2|3-4 duopyramid
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Type||[[duopyramid]]
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|[[Schläfli symbol]]||{3}+{4}

|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|[[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]]||{{CDD|node_f1|3|node|2x|node_f1|4|node}}<BR>{{CDD|node_f1|3|node|2x|node_f1|2x|node_f1}}
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Cells||12 [[digonal disphenoid]]s
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Faces||24 isosceles triangles
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Edges||19 (12+3+4)
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Vertices||7 (3+4)
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|[[Coxeter notation|Symmetry]]||[3,2,4], order 48
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|[[Dual polytope|Dual]]||3-4 duoprism
|-
|bgcolor=#e7dcc3|Properties||[[Convex polytope|convex]], [[facet-transitive]]
|}
The dual of a ''3-4 duoprism'' is called a '''3-4 [[duopyramid]]'''. It has 12 [[digonal disphenoid]] cells, 24  isosceles triangular faces, 12 edges, and 7 vertices.
